title: streaming-sse-chunking-backpressure-debug-notes-alex-kim
content:
Context / summary:
I hit a flaky issue where long-running streamed responses (SSE / streaming tokens from model) sometimes arrive as a single giant chunk or stall mid-stream on clients (JS fetch, curl) and then resume — leading to poor tail latency and client-level backpressure problems. Repro is intermittent in prod but consistent on my local repro when simulating certain network/proxy conditions. This note is a scratchpad of commands tried, server logs, observed errors, hypotheses, and next steps.

Observed symptoms:
- Clients see either very small chunks (1-5 tokens) spaced out (expected) or a sudden large blob (many tokens) delivered at once.
- On Node JS clients, the ReadableStream sometimes blocks and then bursts a large concatenated chunk.
- curl -N sometimes shows no output for ~3s then prints many events in one go.
- When proxying through nginx/ALB, behavior is worse (more buffering).
- No application-level errors, but user-facing request latency/tail percentiles spike.

Commands / repro steps tried: (server is local: http://localhost:8080/stream)
1) Basic curl SSE (unbuffered):
   curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" http://localhost:8080/stream
   - Observed: with no proxy, incremental 'data: <token>' lines appear every ~50-120ms as expected.

2) Repro with nginx reverse proxy (local config with proxy_buffering on/off):
   - nginx config change toggling proxy_buffering: on => large bursts, off => smoother.
   - Command: curl -N http://localhost:8081/stream (nginx -> upstream 8080)
   - Observed: proxy_buffering on collects several chunks then forwards as one. Setting proxy_buffering off reduces bursts but not eliminate.

3) Node Fetch client reading stream:
   const res = await fetch(url, {headers: {Accept: 'text/event-stream'}});
   const reader = res.body.getReader();
   while(true){ const {value, done} = await reader.read(); if(done) break; console.log('chunk len', value.length); }
   - Observed: value lengths vary; sometimes long pause then value length spikes (2500 bytes).

4) Repro with curl + tcpdump to inspect small TCP-level segments:
   sudo tcpdump -i lo -w sse.pcap port 8080
   - Observed: server writes multiple small TLS/TCP packets, but client-visible buffering corresponds to Nagle/coalescing at different layers (proxy, OS).

5) HTTP/2 vs HTTP/1.1 tests:
   - HTTP/2 ALPN often coalesces frames differently; using http2 local server reduces chunk burst frequency (different framing semantics).

6) Simulate slow consumer by reading stream slowly in Node (delay between reads):
   - When client slows, server's Write calls begin to block; server goroutine stack shows syscall write blocking and then returning EAGAIN then resuming.

Error snippets/logs from server / client:
- server logs: "write tcp 127.0.0.1:8080->127.0.0.1:59628: write: broken pipe" (when client disconnects mid-stream)
- client Node error (rare): "ERR_STREAM_WRITE_AFTER_END" (something tries to write after stream closed)
- nginx error log (buffer size overflow): "upstream sent too big header while reading response header from upstream" (not directly related but shows buffering limits being hit)

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Intermediate proxy buffering (nginx, ALB, CloudFront) is the primary cause: by default many proxies buffer responses and only flush when buffer fills or upstream signals flush. SSE with chunked transfer-encoding needs explicit flush semantics.
2) Server-side runtime writes are batched at OS/socket layer (Nagle), and TLS implementation may coalesce TLS records, creating larger visible chunks.
3) The runtime's internal batching (for model token emission) vs flush behavior: if we generate tokens quickly, runtime may group them into one write call to reduce syscalls — but should call flush/flush-like (for Go net/http: use Flusher and ResponseWriter.(Flusher).Flush()).
4) Client-side read semantics: some client libs (fetch polyfills, some HTTP/2 clients) perform internal buffering before exposing data to the JS stream reader.
5) Backpressure signaling mismatch: if the server ignores TCP backpressure (writes with large internal buffers), it can cause writes to succeed quickly then later stall; proper use of non-blocking IO / respecting errors/returns required.

What we've tried to mitigate / results:
- Added explicit Flusher.Flush() after every token write in Go server: improved chunk granularity locally when no proxy, but nginx proxy still bursts unless proxy_buffering off.
- Disabled gzip compression for SSE endpoints: compression was causing buffering until flushes reached compression block sizes. Disabling solved many large-burst cases.
- Set 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' and wrote each event with trailing \n
- Node client: read with small buffer, forced decode streaming via TextDecoder and incremental concatenation to ensure we process partial chunks when available. Slight improvement but doesn't help with proxy-induced bursts.

Repro commands to run for another dev:
1) Start local server (example Go server in /examples/sse): go run ./examples/sse/main.go
2) Plain client: curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" http://localhost:8080/stream
3) Through nginx: start nginx with provided conf (nginx/nginx-stream-tests.conf) and run: curl -v -N http://localhost:8081/stream
4) tcpdump to inspect timings: sudo tcpdump -i lo -A 'tcp port 8080' > sse.dump & then run client and inspect timestamps.

Notes on root cause candidates and immediate fixes:
- If proxy buffering is the issue: document that SSE endpoint must set headers to disable buffering where possible (for nginx: proxy_buffering off; for upstream LB: configure socket buffer/enable chunked encoding and disable response buffering). For Cloud load balancers, check if they have 'streaming' mode.
- If TLS/coalescing is an issue: consider calling TLSConn.Flush (where supported) or send application-level heartbeat events more frequently to force record boundaries.
- Compression: avoid gzip for streaming endpoints or use 'gzip: off' for those routes.
- Runtime level: ensure we call ResponseWriter.(http.Flusher).Flush() after each event. For frameworks that abstract away net/http, confirm they expose flush.

Open questions / next steps:
- Quantify how much each layer (app, OS, proxy) contributes: instrument with timestamps at server write, kernel send, proxy receive, proxy send, client receive.
- Review ALB/NLB docs for buffering behavior with chunked + keep-alive.
- Add a small integration test that starts nginx with varying proxy_buffering and verifies event inter-arrival times.
- Consider adding a server config toggle 'sse.flush_mode' to force unconditional flush and to disable compression.

Scratchpad: quick commands to run locally
- curl: curl -v -N -H "Accept: text/event-stream" http://localhost:8080/stream
- curl via nginx (nginx must be running locally): curl -v -N http://localhost:8081/stream
- Node snippet: (paste into node REPL)
  const fetch = require('node-fetch');
  (async ()=>{ const res = await fetch('http://localhost:8080/stream',{headers:{Accept:'text/event-stream'}}); const rd = res.body.getReader(); const td = new TextDecoder(); while(true){ const {value,done}=await rd.read(); if(done)break; console.log(Date.now(), td.decode(value)); await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,20)); }} )();

If anyone sees additional angles (kernel TCP_FASTOPEN, socket cork options, or specific ALB/nginx flags), ping me. Will follow up with a small integration/automated test once we have a deterministic repro.

-- Alex
